source.title: Enforcing Orderedness to Improve Feature Consistency
source.authors: Sophie L. Wang; Alex Quach; Nithin Parsan; John J. Yang

page_placements.theme: Nested-prefix (Matryoshka-type) objectives order latents by granularity

record.tranche_reason: The paper's SAE-stitching results refine the claim about cross-size feature completeness: larger-SAE features are classified as novel at nonzero rates, but the rates differ by SAE type and are lower for O-SAE than for BatchTopK.
record.gate_note: The main experiments measure feature stability and orderedness across seeds, datasets, and dictionary prefixes; they do not measure coarse-to-fine feature splitting, input partitioning, or nearby feature directions. The Appendix D stitching experiment is the paper's own result relevant to V5. Other results, including cited findings, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Appendix D reuses the SAE-stitching procedure of an original V5 source (Leask et al.). It stitches 65536-width latents into 4096-width SAEs and classifies each as novel (lowers MSE) or reconstruction (raises MSE, overlaps existing latents). This is done for BatchTopK, Random MSAE and O-SAE. The main-text results (seed and dataset stability, orderedness) do not measure splitting and are fits_no_version material.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim O-SAEs 'substantially reduce' novel features via stitching and frame this as more complete decompositions. They also say increasing hierarchy lowers the novel percentage. Their wording that O-SAEs 'close those gaps' overstates a 33.8% novel rate, which they themselves call substantial.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces an ordered nested-prefix SAE objective and evaluates cross-seed feature stability and ordering. Its stitching experiment follows a feature-insertion and reconstruction-based evaluation; it does not reproduce the original feature-splitting measurement of matched directions and input partitions.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that orderedness and stability depend on design choices including the prefix distribution and unit sweeping. These choices concern its consistency experiments, not the stitching outcomes recorded here.

fits_no_version.finding: A fraction of stitched latents produce no MSE change: 5.0% BatchTopK, 35.9% Random MSAE, 1.4% O-SAE. The authors link the Random MSAE share partly to non-activating features on limited samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some larger-SAE latents are inert when stitched into a smaller SAE, at rates that depend on the SAE objective.

fits_no_version.finding: O-SAEs give higher cross-seed orderedness and early-prefix stability than Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2 2B and Pythia-70M, and on a Gaussian toy model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ordered nested-prefix objectives improve the cross-seed consistency and ordering of SAE latents.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
record.problems: The stitching table does not state the underlying model or uncertainty, and it tests only one source-to-target size pair. Stitching classifications are an indirect proxy: they do not directly establish geometric decomposition of larger latents into smaller ones. The paper notes that O-SAE still has a substantial novel-feature fraction.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing directly on the tested V5 component were left out. Consistency and orderedness results in the main text and appendices were omitted because they do not measure feature splitting or the V5 stitching outcomes.

untested.parts: Direct decomposition of larger latents into combinations of smaller latents (e.g. meta-SAE). Claims about no dictionary size being complete, beyond the single 65536→4096 pair.
Coarse-to-fine splitting, input coverage and direction proximity are not measured.
Not measured; hierarchy is only invoked as a training prior.
Splitting under alternative objectives is not measured. The stitching table shows the objective changes the novel-latent fraction, not splitting itself.

missing.what: The model, layer, sample count and number of latents stitched for Table 2 are unstated. Rows should record 'not stated', and researchers need this to compare with Leask et al.

record.verdict_notes: The stitching evidence comes from one width pair with no uncertainty, model or layer reported, and it is an appendix result. The reconstruction category is linked to V5 only as indirect evidence of overlap, not proof of compositional decomposition. V6 is left untested: the objective changes the novel-latent fraction, not splitting as such.

versions.untested_parts: The stitching results report novel-feature classifications, but do not directly test whether larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller-SAE latents or establish that no dictionary size yields a complete atomic set.

tranche.reason: Appendix D reuses Leask et al.'s SAE-stitching procedure and its novel/reconstruction categories, the original's method and measure for V5.

source_check.notes: Appendix D never names the model, layer, sample count or number of stitched latents. Main-text SAEs on Gemma-2 2B (layer 12) and Pythia-70M (layer 3) are both 4096-wide, so either could be the target. Table 2 gives no seeds or uncertainty. Random MSAE has more non-activating features on the limited samples, which inflates its 35.9% no-MSE-change share. The authors' claim that O-SAEs 'close those gaps' sits uneasily with their own 33.8% novel share.

statements.correction: Table 2: novel share 73.8/52.7/33.8% shows the 4096 SAE is incomplete relative to the 65536 SAE (authors: 'strong incompleteness' for BatchTopK). Reconstruction share 21.2/11.4/64.8% = overlap with existing small-SAE latents, not incompleteness of the larger SAE. No test of the 65536 SAE's completeness.
statements.problem: 'so neither width is complete' overreaches: stitching shows only that the 4096 SAE lacks information the 65536 SAE has; the 65536 SAE's completeness is untested.

statements.correction: Gemma-2 2B: O-SAE Ord(D,D') above Fixed and Random MSAE; overall stability lower, higher for most significant features. Pythia-70M (Fig. 3a): orderedness higher after prefix 128; early stability above Random MSAE, but Fixed MSAE stability higher than O-SAE. Gaussian toy (Table 1): Stab(D,D') 0.664 vs 0.538/0.531; Ord(D,D*) 0.734 vs 0.119/0.054.
statements.problem: No-MSE-change numbers right, but f1 summary overgeneralises: on Pythia-70M Fixed MSAE has higher stability than O-SAE; the Gaussian toy reports ground-truth orderedness and full-dictionary cross-seed stability, not cross-seed orderedness or prefix stability.
